# PREFACE.

Among all the truths confessed by our Church, there is none about which there is more obscurity than the nature of the Church; not so much regarding what we understand by the universal Christian Church, which shall be eternally saved, but concerning the **visible Church**, as it consists of the called and the <term>chosen<note>Also referred to as the "elect" in Reformed theology—those predestined by God for salvation.</note></term>. There is nothing more common to read among contemporary <term>theologians<note>Original Dutch: "Godsgeleerden," literally those learned in God.</note></term> than that the one true Church consists only of the multitude of chosen believers who, bought by Jesus' blood and most closely united with Him, shall be eternally saved—beginning here and continuing hereafter; and then to distinguish this into a **visible** and **invisible** Church. 

However, one immediately adds that this must not be understood as if there were a visible Church consisting of different persons than the invisible one, but rather that the Church is so named in a twofold respect. First, we call the Church **invisible** insofar as the true <term>change of heart<note>Original Dutch: "herts-verandering." This refers to the internal spiritual transformation or "regeneration" that a person undergoes, which is not outwardly visible to the human eye.</note></term>, which constitutes a true and properly defined member of the Church, is not infallibly certain

<summary>This preface introduces a theological examination of the Church's nature, specifically addressing the common but often misunderstood distinction between the "visible" and "invisible" Church. The author argues that while the true Church consists of the elect, the labels "visible" and "invisible" refer to different ways of perceiving the same body of believers.</summary>

<keywords>Ecclesiology, Visible Church, Invisible Church, Theology, Election, Salvation, Regeneration, Membership</keywords>

This refers to the inner spiritual state of an individual, which remains concealed from others.</note></term>, known only to the <term>Searcher of Hearts<note>Original Dutch: "Hertenkenner." A traditional theological title for God, who alone possesses the power to see into a person's soul.</note></term>, 2 Timothy 2:19. But it is visible insofar as that person gives outward signs of a true change of heart, and lets his light shine before men, from which we morally—according to the <term>judgment of charity<note>Original Dutch: "oordeel der lievde." This is a theological principle where one assumes the best about another's spiritual state based on their outward behavior, even if one cannot see their heart.</note></term>—consider him a pious Christian, and as such practice the communion of saints with him. Among these join many who make a pure confession of the true religion and display an appearance of godliness, but lacking the internal change of heart, they are indeed held by us to be members of the **visible Church**, because we are not searchers of hearts; yet they are truly in no way members of the visible Church, but **hypocrites** or pretenders, who wish to be held as those who have received grace. We cannot refuse to give them the name of **Members**, yet they belong to it as little as harlots in a convent belong to the virgins, or traitors and foreign residents living in a city belong to the citizens. Were it otherwise, we would make two Churches of it, or change the true Church into an <term>Antichristian monster<note>A polemical term used to suggest that if the Church were defined by both the ungodly and the godly as equal members, it would lose its holy nature and become a grotesque distortion of Christ's intent.</note></term>. ...[has] stood and been protected; [the Church is] invisible when she is suppressed by heresies, persecutions... so that true believers do not dare to come forward for the truth, and do not show their internal <term>godliness<note>Original Dutch: "Godzaligheid." This refers to an inward state of piety and devotion to God that may not always be visible to external observers during times of danger.</note></term>. As is commonly proven from the time of <term>Elijah<note>A reference to 1 Kings 19, where the prophet Elijah feels he is the last faithful follower of God in Israel.</note></term>, when he believed himself to be the only one remaining, while there were still seven thousand who had not bowed their knees to <term>Baal<note>A Canaanite deity; in this context, bowing to Baal represents falling away into idolatry or false worship.</note></term>, which is understood to refer to those truly favored by grace; and under the New Testament, when she <note>the Church</note>, sighing under the yoke of the <term>Antichrist<note>In the context of this period’s Protestant theology, this often referred to the perceived corruptions of the Roman Church or any worldly power that persecuted the "true" faith.</note></term>, was like a fleeing woman in the wilderness.

This is a thought originating from a confused understanding of the nature of the <term>Covenant of Grace<note>Original Dutch: "Genade-verbond." The theological framework describing God's promise of eternal life through Jesus Christ.</note></term>, by which one understands—especially under the New Testament—that agreement between God and the elect sinner, whereby the latter, in a soul-saving manner, accepts Christ offered to him, and solemnly binds himself to God, and actually becomes a partaker of God's gracious benefits promised in the covenant. But others, who indeed agree with the content of the covenant of grace as the only true way to salvation and make a confession of it, are in no way <term>covenant-members<note>Original Dutch: "bond-genooten." Literally "covenant-allies" or "partners," referring to those who are truly part of the spiritual contract with God.</note></term>. If they are not covenant-members, the <term>covenant-seals<note>Original Dutch: "bond-zegelen." This refers to the sacraments, specifically Baptism and the Lord's Supper, which serve as visible confirmations of the invisible covenant.</note></term> do not belong to them either, for those are never given except to covenant-members; indeed, the promises of the covenant do not belong to them either:

# Historical Narrative

# ...of the Labadists.

Now the work began of establishing a new and pure Church. *Labadie*, having come to live in *Amsterdam*, sent out his disciples to persuade some of the godly members of the Dutch Church toward separation. These disciples then did their best in *Utrecht*, in *The Hague*, in *Middelburg*, in *Dordrecht* <note>original: "Dorth"</note>, and *Amsterdam* to proceed with the foundations and teachings of separation. This was in the year 1673; in which year Miss *Schuurman* <note>Anna Maria van Schuurman (1607–1678) was a Dutch painter, poet, and scholar. (a) She wrote that little book in Latin, and named it *The Better Part of A. ## of the Labadists.

...rn, <note>The Dutch text begins with "leeren," completing the sentence from the previous page: "I wished only to show them how to better learn..."</note> according to the Book of the wise and spiritual practitioner *Mr. Brown* <note>Referring to John Brown of Wamphray (c. 1610–1679), a Scottish Presbyterian theologian whose work "Christ the Way, the Truth, and the Life" was popular in the Netherlands.</note>, titled *Christ the Way*, or according to another, titled, *The Christian's Great Interest*, written by *Mr. William Guthrie* <note>William Guthrie (1620–1665) was another influential Scottish Covenanter; his work "The Christian's Great Interest" was a staple of Reformed practical divinity.</note>.

*The Thirty-third Error.* That the works of the "first conversion," as they call them (a) (that is, of a soul that is merely being disposed and prepared, and yet has not been brought to Christ through a living faith) are pleasing to God; and that the Holy Spirit also comforts such individuals. This is a blunt error against the foundations of the Reformed Religion; for an unconverted person who is outside of Christ is not pleasing to God, and it is impossible that he should be pleasing to God, since he does not yet have faith, according to *Hebrews 11:6*. And as long as the person is not pleasing <note>In Reformed theology, the "person" must be justified (accepted) before their "works" can be considered good.</note>, his works cannot be pleasing; likewise, there is no true comfort of the Holy Spirit when one is outside of Christ. Their proofs taken from *Isaiah 66:2, Psalm 51:19, and 2 Corinthians 7:10* are misapplied. For those passages do not speak of a soul that is outside of faith; this <note>this error</note> is the consequence of their preceding error, and yet these are the people who claim they will best work souls toward godliness <term>Godzaligheid: a state of living in accordance with God's will; piety</term>.

*...separate meetings, says Voetius* <note>Gijsbertus Voetius (1589–1676) was a highly influential Dutch Reformed theologian and a lead proponent of "Further Reformation" (Nadere Reformatie) who nonetheless opposed the radical separatism of the Labadists.</note>, *except when:* 1. *The Papists* <term>Papists</term> <note>A historical, often pejorative term for Roman Catholics, referring to their loyalty to the Pope.</note> *had made all hope of reformation impossible.* 2. *The people, and also the Magistrates, awakened by the preaching of the Gospel, had flocked together to the raised banner.* 3. *The lightning bolts of excommunication and tyranny cast out the orthodox Teachers and students from their previous assemblies.* 4. *Through the Inquisition, no one could remain under the Papacy without having positive and active fellowship in that horrible idolatry in the Mass.* <note>The Reformed tradition viewed the Catholic Mass as "idolatry" primarily because of the doctrine of transubstantiation and the veneration of the host.</note> Even Labadie <note>Jean de Labadie (1610–1674), a former Jesuit turned Reformed minister who eventually founded the separatist Labadist movement.</note> did not immediately leave the Roman Church when he recognized her manifold defects and heresies, but for many years more he sought to heal that incurable *Babel* <note>A common Protestant metaphor for the Roman Catholic Church, implying it was a site of spiritual confusion and corruption beyond repair.</note>, until he had to flee from there to save his life. *Fourthly.* They did not properly arm or concern themselves with avoiding falling into errors in theory and practice, while they sought a holy Church and the holiness of their persons. 2. *Argument*. Because the Apostle says *vs. 28. Let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread, etc.* (a) And so he shows two things. 1. ### Of the Labadists

<page-num>305</page-num>
<header>of the Labadists.</header>

...examine <note>The Dutch text begins mid-word with "-ven onderzoeken," completing the thought from the previous page regarding the command to examine oneself.</note>, and so let him eat; that is, when someone has overseen his own state in all sincerity and has obtained a suitable readiness for the Lord's Supper in regard to his own spiritual condition, he must then eat, without looking to the state of others. Otherwise, even if someone had examined himself and his condition was as it should be, he would still be unable to eat if the unfitness of others could prevent him from eating. But the Apostle intends to intentionally exclude that by linking those two things or commands together: namely, *man’s eating* with the *testing of himself*. Thus, a person may—indeed, he must—partake of the Holy Supper once he has examined himself, even if he takes no account of the spiritual state of other <term>communicants</term> <note>Those who receive the sacrament of the Lord's Supper together.</note>; for the command to *eat* is just as absolute as the command to *examine*.

3. *Argument*. Because the Apostle says in *verse 29*, (a) *whoever eats and drinks unworthily, eats and drinks judgment to himself*; he does not say that such a person eats and drinks judgment upon his fellow communicants, which would nevertheless be the case if the admission of such people made communicating unlawful for the pious.

<margin>(a) See Calvin’s *Institutes*, Book 4, Chapter 1, Section 15. <note>John Calvin (1509–1564) was a central figure in the Reformation; his *Institutes of the Christian Religion* is a foundational work of Protestant theology.</note></margin>

Therefore, no one else has a reason to stay away from the <term>Lord’s Supper</term> <note>The Dutch *Avondmaal* (Evening Meal) refers to the sacrament of Holy Communion.</note> for that reason, provided he has tested himself. 4. *Argument.* Because the Apostle says in *verse 31: For if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged*; that is, in this case, people need not be anxious about whether others test themselves well or not: for, he says, God's acquittal or judgment of us does not depend...

1. *Argument.* Because the churches have always believed that the relative covenantal holiness <note>A status of being "set apart" due to being part of a community in a contract with God, rather than personal holiness.</note> of the children of those who profess faith (according to *1 Cor. 7:14*) is immediately sufficient to partake in membership within the visible Church; for this reason, they have always baptized without hesitation the children born within the boundaries of the visible Church, as being immediately within the covenant and members of the church, not based on their personal or saving grace, but on their relative holiness, derived from the parents who profess faith, whether those parents are reborn or not.

2. *Argument.* Because in their preaching as well as in their writing, they have constantly and beforehand established that people can openly break their covenant with God; thus, they must first be outwardly within the covenant and members of the visible Church to be capable of breaking that bond.

3. *Argument.* Because they have generally believed and judged that notorious ungodly and offensive people are within the church until such time as they are <term>censured</term> <note>original: "gecenſureert." Subjected to formal church discipline or correction.</note> and entirely cast out.

**Key Vocabulary from this section:**
- **Visible Church:** The external, organized body of believers and their children, as seen by people.
- **Saving grace:** The internal work of the Holy Spirit that leads to eternal salvation.
- **Unregenerate:** A person who has not been spiritually made new.
- **Professors/Confessors:** Those who openly declare their belief in Christian doctrine.
- **Covenantal holiness:** The status of being included in God's promises through the church community.
- **Membership:** The state of belonging to the church body.
- **Censured:** Formally disciplined by the church leadership for misconduct or heresy.

### CHAPTER V.

**Further Proofs that the Covenant with Israel was, in its substance, the Covenant of Grace, and not merely a fleshly Covenant; with the resolution of the principal *Objections*.**

Since the errors of the *Labadists* <note>The Labadists were a 17th-century radical Pietist sect founded by Jean de Labadie. They sought to form a "community of saints" and often emphasized a sharp distinction between the Old and New Testaments, which the author here contests.</note> particularly rest upon a false notion that God did not establish the covenant of grace with Israel, we shall further prove the opposite with the following reasons, and then resolve the contrary arguments.

<margin>*Leviticus* 11:45. *Leviticus* 22:33. *Leviticus* 25:38.</margin>
1. *Proof.* That covenant—in and through which those covenant-members who were faithful were promised and given the same blessings that are promised in the covenant of grace and granted to believers under the New Testament—is in its substance the covenant of grace. Now, such is the Israelite covenant; which is evident, 1. Because God has been their God, just as He is ours who live under the New Covenant; and that one promise <note>The phrase "to be their God" is treated by Reformed theologians as the "soul" of the covenant, containing all spiritual promises.</note> encompasses all spiritual and saving blessings.

### The Errors of the Labadists Refuted.

*The greatest multitude of the people of Israel had no part in the grace of the covenant acquired by Christ; therefore, they were not in the covenant.* (Yvon, *On the Covenants* <note>original: "De Fœderibus"</note> page 125.)
*Answer:* This proves what we do not deny, namely that the majority were not in that covenant *inwardly*, but only *outwardly* through an external confession. ### The Covenant with Israel Was Not Merely Physical.

> *Verse 23. But the one who was from the bondwoman was born according to the flesh; but this one who was from the free woman, through the promise.*

Here the Apostle brings before our eyes the illustrative history of *Abraham's* household, taken from *Genesis* 16 and 21, of which this is the short summary: That just as *Abraham* had two sons, namely *Ishmael* and *Isaac* (he had several others by *Keturah*, *Gen.* 25:2, but those two are only recounted as having been ordained by God to serve as a foreshadowing <term>foreshadowing: A theological concept, often called "typology," where Old Testament figures or events are seen as symbols that predict or explain New Testament truths.</term> of the present), the status of these two sons differed in two ways. First, that the one, *Ishmael*, was born of a slave or bondwoman, namely *Hagar*, *Gen.* 16:1, 15, and thus he himself was only as a bondservant, and not the heir, <note>Being born to a slave woman meant that, according to ancient law, the child inherited the mother's status of servitude rather than the father's status of wealth and freedom.</note> *Gen.* 21:10. The other, namely *Isaac*, was born of a free woman, namely of *Sarah*, *Gen.* 21:2, 3, who had never been a bondwoman, but had always been the Wife and co-regent of the Household with her Husband; and therefore *Isaac* was no bondservant, but a free man, indeed the heir. A second distinction lay in the fundamental principle of their generation and birth: for *Ishmael* was born according to the flesh <note>The phrase "according to the flesh" implies a natural birth without divine intervention, whereas Isaac's birth was considered miraculous because of his parents' old age.</note>...

*manner; whether the Church is considered internally, or its external appearance is viewed, the same thing regarding its essence appears to us.* OBSERVATION 1. <term>Yvon</term> <note>Pierre Yvon (1646–1707) was the successor to Jean de Labadie and the primary writer defending the Labadist movement, which insisted that only the truly "born again" should be members of the church.</note> misrepresents our view and thus deceives the reader: For he suggests that our side posits two distinct covenants—an outward covenant, to which one part of the Church is relegated or "sent off," as he puts it, and an inward covenant, in which the <term>regenerate</term> <note>In Reformed theology, the "regenerate" are those whose hearts have been spiritually renewed by God, as opposed to "professors" who belong to the church through outward words only.</note> reside. However, we do not posit two covenants, but only one covenant, the <term>Covenant of Grace</term> <note>The Covenant of Grace is the theological concept that God enters into a relationship with humanity based on His mercy through Christ, rather than human merit.</note>; which covenant is either made and consented to outwardly by the <term>Profession</term> <note>A "profession" is the public declaration of faith required for church membership.</note> of men with God, or is additionally confirmed inwardly in the soul. Those who are in that covenant inwardly are also in it outwardly; but the reverse is not always true. Whether Yvon makes this false representation out of pure ignorance, or from a more sinister root, he must examine for himself. 2. To make this matter clearer, which Yvon so obscures, I shall attempt to make it understood through a comparison with a mutual covenant among men. No one will find it difficult to understand or admit that two different types of persons can enter into a covenant or <term>alliance</term> <note>original: "alliantie"</note> with a third party, and make with him the same covenant on the same conditions, and agree to those specified conditions, and provide testimony and signature and sealing, *(which I call professing for the purpose of sealing,)* even though the conditions, when the covenant is made mutually, have not yet been fulfilled, and even though one person thinks he can and will keep the covenant and meet the condition by his own strength and means—or at least is not so hearty and sincere in his core—while the other, on the contrary, being more upright, looked to the help that would be granted to him from the outside. In this case, the covenant is truly made (with both); they have entered into that same covenant with that third party, and they are bound to him by their consent as his <term>Covenant-partners</term>. Yet only one (by whose help it also comes) fulfills the condition and receives the promised benefits from the third party; and the other does not fulfill the condition, even though by consenting to it he had freely declared he would fulfill it. Therefore, he is a <term>covenant-breaker</term> <note>original: "verbond-breeker"</note>, and will be punished by that third party accordingly; which could not be the case if the covenant with that third party had not actually been made in fact.

...which was the opinion of the (a) <term>Antinomians</term><note>original: "Antinomi"; a theological movement (most prominent in 17th-century England) that argued that because Christians are saved by grace alone, they are not bound by the moral laws of the Old Testament. It is also against the nature of a <term>covenant</term><note>original: "verbond"; in Reformed theology, the "Covenant of Grace" is the legal and spiritual framework of God's relationship with humanity. The author argues that like a legal contract, it involves two parties with mutual obligations.</note>, which is something other than a promise without any condition; for it is an agreement between various parties, binding themselves together on mutual conditions required of both parties—as between Abraham and Abimelech, *Gen. 20*, and between God and Abraham, *Gen. 17*. God not only promises the covenant, *Deut. 7:12*, but he also commands the covenant, *Josh. 7:11*, which is the condition required on our side. God also brings the people into the bond of the covenant, *Ezek. 20:37*, and he binds them to himself through the covenant, as if with a belt, *Jer. 13:11*, so that they become servants to him, *1 Cor. 7:22*. Thus, there is indeed a condition to the covenant as it is preached; and so we are sometimes said to keep the covenant with God, *Ps. 25:10, Psalm 103:18,* and sometimes to break...
